sections.title: Overview
blocks: Nails grow slowly and record what has happened to the matrix and nail bed over months. Many nail signs are clues to skin disease (psoriasis, eczema, lichen planus) or systemic disease (illness, drugs, lung, heart, liver or bowel disease).

ul: **Matrix** disease changes the nail plate: pits, ridges, Beau’s lines, leukonychia.
**Nail-bed** disease changes how the plate attaches and its colour: onycholysis, oil-drop patches, splinter haemorrhages, subungual thickening.
**Clubbing** reflects soft-tissue overgrowth of the fingertip, thought to be driven by platelet-derived growth factors bypassing the lung capillaries.
**"White spots mean calcium deficiency"**: they are usually minor trauma.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: Where the damage is in the nail unit **decides the sign**.

mech.t: The matrix makes the plate; damage changes the plate surface (pits, Beau's lines).
The bed anchors the plate; inflammation lifts it (onycholysis).
Splinters are bed capillary bleeds along longitudinal ridges.
Fingertip soft tissue grows, possibly from platelet-derived growth factors bypassing the lung.

mech.caption: A longitudinal band begins in the matrix.

sections.title: Clinical features
blocks: **Matrix disease:** irregular **pitting**, leukonychia, red lunula spots, Beau lines, crumbling. **Nail-bed disease:** **onycholysis**, oil-drop/salmon patches, subungual hyperkeratosis, splinter haemorrhages. Often coexists with skin/scalp/genital psoriasis or psoriatic arthritis — examine beyond the nail. DDx onychomycosis (mycology if treating as fungus). Management is that of psoriasis (topicals, systemic/biologic pathways via dermatology) — deepen in **Module 4**.

Transverse **depressions** across the nail (often multiple nails at same level) after temporary **arrest of matrix growth** — severe systemic illness, high fever, chemotherapy, childbirth, major stressor. Grow out with the nail (fingernails ~3–4 mm/month rough guide). Usually no specific nail drug therapy — explain and date the insult. Multiple waves can mark repeated insults.

**Clubbing:** increased nail-fold soft tissue, increased nail curvature, **loss of Lovibond angle** (<165° normally preserved), often boggy nail bed. Associated with lung cancer, interstitial lung disease, bronchiectasis/abscess, cyanotic heart disease, IBD, cirrhosis, and other systemic diseases; also hypertrophic osteoarthropathy.

**IP action:** recognise → **history/exam for cardiopulmonary/GI red flags** → urgent appropriate medical referral/investigation — **not** a dermatology cream problem. Congenital/familial clubbing exists but new clubbing in adults is sinister until proven otherwise.

ul: Look at **all 20 nails**, the skin, scalp and joints.
Ask about recent illness, chemotherapy, new drugs, trauma, wet work and nail cosmetics.
Send clippings if fungal infection is possible, because psoriasis and onychomycosis can look identical and can coexist.
For clubbing, check Schamroth’s window (lost diamond-shaped gap when the backs of two fingertips are pressed together) and look for chest, cardiac, liver or bowel signs.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: **New clubbing**: same-week GP review for chest, cardiac, liver or bowel causes; chest X-ray is often the first test.
Nail psoriasis with joint pain or dactylitis: screen for **psoriatic arthritis** (PEST) and refer to rheumatology.
Changes grow out over 6 months (fingers) to 12–18 months (toes).

pearls: Dating a Beau’s line: fingernails grow about 3 mm a month, so a line 6 mm from the cuticle marks an event about 2 months ago.
Nail psoriasis predicts psoriatic arthritis: ask about joint pain and morning stiffness at every review.
Treat nail psoriasis expectations carefully: improvement takes months, and topical treatment works best on the nail folds.

quiz.q: When should you think of Nail signs: psoriatic nails, Beau’s lines & clubbing?
quiz.a: Pits, oil-drop patches, lifting nails, transverse grooves, or a bulbous fingertip.
Psoriasis in the nail matrix and bed; a temporary halt in nail growth (Beau’s lines); tissue proliferation in clubbing.

quiz.q: What is the backbone of care?
quiz.a: Link the nail to the whole patient: joints for psoriasis, recent illness or drugs for Beau’s lines, a systemic review for clubbing.
New clubbing (lung cancer, fibrosis, endocarditis, IBD, cirrhosis).
